questions.question: When does the lesson recommend using a Stream instead of `%String`?

options.text: Only for boolean values
When content may exceed about 1MB or has no fixed size
Only when the class is abstract
Only inside SQL queries

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the lesson's rule of thumb is to use streams for large or unbounded content such as uploads, large JSON, XML, or HTML.

questions.question: Which class is the most common choice for large text content stored in IRIS globals?

options.text: %Stream.GlobalCharacter
%Stream.GlobalBinary
%Stream.FileBinary
%String

questions.explanation: T1.2 — `%Stream.GlobalCharacter` is the documented stream class for text stored in IRIS globals.

questions.question: You need to store a PDF attachment as a stream property in a persistent class. Which type is the best fit?

options.text: %Stream.GlobalCharacter
%Stream.GlobalBinary
%Stream.FileCharacter
%String(MAXLEN = 0)

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the lesson maps `%Stream.GlobalBinary` to binary content such as images, PDFs, and other files.

questions.question: Which statement about size limits is correct?

options.text: `%String` has no practical limit, but streams do.
Streams are limited to 32KB, but `%String` is unlimited.
`%String` is limited to about 3.6MB, while streams are effectively unlimited.
Both `%String` and streams share the same 3.6MB limit.

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the lesson contrasts `%String` at about 3,641,144 characters with streams, which are used for unbounded content.

questions.question: Which pattern does the lesson recommend for reading very large stream content safely?

options.text: Always call `Read()` once with no argument, regardless of size.
Use a loop with `While 'stream.AtEnd { Set chunk = stream.Read(32000) }`.
Convert the stream to an array and use `$ORDER`.
Use `%OpenId()` on the stream itself for each chunk.

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the key point recommends chunked reads with `AtEnd` and `Read(32000)` for very large content.

questions.question: In a REST endpoint, what does `%request.Content` represent according to the lesson?

options.text: A pre-parsed dynamic object
A normal `%String` variable
A stream containing the request body
A query plan object

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the REST section states that `%request.Content` is already a stream, so you can rewind and read it.

questions.question: What does `SET sc = dest.CopyFrom(source)` do?

options.text: It converts the source stream into a SQL query.
It copies the content of one stream into another stream.
It rewinds both streams automatically and saves them.
It creates a bitmap index for the stream.

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the copying section explicitly shows `CopyFrom(source)` as the way to copy one stream into another.

questions.question: Which statements about streams are correct? (select all that apply)

options.text: Stream data is stored in separate stream globals rather than inline like a small `%String`.
`%request.Content` is already a stream in REST handlers.
Reading a huge stream all at once can use a lot of memory.
`%Stream.FileCharacter` is used for text stored on the filesystem.
`%String` has the same unlimited capacity as streams.

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the lesson contrasts inline `%String` storage with separate stream storage, notes `%request.Content` is a stream, warns about large `Read()` calls, and lists file-based stream classes.

questions.question: Which snippets are valid stream-related patterns from the lesson? (select all that apply)

options.text: Property Content As %Stream.GlobalCharacter;
DO myStream.Write(myString)
SET str = myStream.Read()
DO myStream.Rewind()
SET requestBody = %request.Content

questions.explanation: T1.2 — all of these examples appear in the lesson as valid stream declarations or usage patterns, with the note that reading into a string is safe only when content is small enough.

questions.question: According to the lesson's key points, what should you do after writing to a stream and before reading it again from the beginning?

options.text: Call `%Save()` on the stream object itself
Use `$ORDER()` to reset the stream
Call `Rewind()`
Convert the stream into JSON first

questions.explanation: T1.2 — the lesson explicitly warns that stream position does not reset automatically, so `Rewind()` is needed before reading from the beginning again.
